newsitem.title: USA: U.S. heating oil prices may have peaked, experts say.
newsitem.headline: U.S. heating oil prices may have peaked, experts say.

text.p: After fears of a home heating oil shortage sent prices skyrocketing last month, heating oil retailers say prices have peaked now that refiners have proven they can meet demand.

"My guess is, even if there is some colder-than-normal weather, it seems to be that prices have peaked for the winter," said Robert Greenes, spokesman for New York Oil Heating Association Inc., a heating oil retailers trade group.
Refiners have increased heating oil inventories by almost six million barrels in the last three weeks in the U.S. Northeast, the world's largest heating oil market.
This eased concerns that refiners would not be able to replenish stocks quickly enough ahead of wintery cold snaps.
The average price for a gallon of heating oil in Massachusetts is now $1.12, almost 20 cents more than a year ago.

The high price reflects what retailers had to pay for heating oil futures in October on the New York Mercantile Exchange when prices hit a post-Gulf War high of 76.75 cents a gallon. On Wednesday, heating oil hovered at 69.90 cents.

"It's a fair assessment that dealers have filled their tanks to a point where we have reached a level of security that we haven't had in the past year," said Jack Sullivan, head of the New England Fuel Institute, a Massachusetts group that represents 1,400 heating oil retailers and wholesalers.
Alfred Allegretti, president of Bayside Fuel Oil Depot Corp., a major retailer and wholesaler of heating oil based in Brooklyn, N.Y., said a shortage was never a real threat.
"It was a just big scare," he said, adding: "Refiners have proven themselves extremely flexible, and we have plenty of supplies now."

Economists and dealers said the spike in heating oil prices assumed the possibility of shortage during the winter, enabling heating oil to fetch retail prices in November normally not seen until the thick of winter in January.

"I think the high price is already in the market. Given an average winter, I think prices would have a difficult time advancing since we got the seasonal price rise early," said John Paul Murphy, senior economist at the Massachusetts state energy office.

Cheryl Trench, an economist with the Petroleum Industry Research Foundation, doubts heating oil futures on NYMEX will hit the high level again this winter, barring a prolonged spell of unusually cold weather. "The notion that prices have topped is probably correct, though we may get another spike if there is a cold snap."
But Trench also warned that prices could shoot up if there is a supply disruption at any one of a number of refiners, which are now producing at a feverish pace to meet current demand.
Because this "just-in-time" output programme is relatively new to the oil industry, there is remaining uncertainty as to whether refiners would be able to produce enough in a real pinch.
